title: How to Use INDEX MATCH in Excel (with Examples)
dek: INDEX MATCH is the flexible lookup that fixes VLOOKUP's biggest limits — it can look to the left and it does not break when you add columns. Here is exactly how INDEX and MATCH work together, step by step.

body.richText: Point MATCH at a cell instead of typing the value: =INDEX(B2:B100, MATCH(D1, A2:A100, 0)) returns the price for whatever product you type in D1. That turns one formula into a reusable lookup box.

body.text: Why use it instead of VLOOKUP?

items: VLOOKUP can only return values to the right of the search column. INDEX MATCH can return a value from any column, in either direction.
VLOOKUP breaks when you insert a column, because its column number is hard-coded. INDEX MATCH points at real ranges, so it keeps working.
On large sheets, INDEX MATCH reads only the two columns it needs, not the whole table.

items.question: Is INDEX MATCH better than VLOOKUP?
items.answerRichText: For most real work, yes. INDEX MATCH can look to the left, does not break when you add or move columns, and can be faster on large sheets. VLOOKUP is simpler to type, so it is still fine for quick, one-off lookups on a stable table.

items.question: What does the 0 mean in MATCH?
items.answerRichText: The 0 tells MATCH to find an exact match. Without it, MATCH assumes your data is sorted and looks for the closest lower value, which gives wrong results on unsorted lists. For lookups, always use 0.

items.question: Why does my INDEX MATCH return #N/A?
items.answerRichText: #N/A means MATCH could not find the value. Check for trailing spaces, text stored as numbers, or a lookup range that does not include the value. Make sure the value you are searching for exactly matches the data.

items.question: Can I use INDEX MATCH across two sheets?
items.answerRichText: Yes. Point the ranges at the other sheet, like =INDEX(Data!B2:B100, MATCH(D1, Data!A2:A100, 0)). The formula works exactly the same way when the lookup table lives on a different tab.
